growth_story.headline: Eswatini's income per person has grown a steady 2.4 percent a year since 1990, without regaining the investment that left when apartheid sanctions ended.
growth_story.arc: The data show one era since 1990: income per person grew 2.4 percent a year on average over 1990–2025, with no lasting shift. The sources start the story earlier, in the 1980s, when firms moved to Eswatini to get around sanctions on apartheid South Africa. After sanctions ended in 1994 many firms moved back, and income per person grew no faster than 1.8 percent a year from 1996 to 2001. Growth then ran between 3.0 and 6.2 percent a year in 2002–2007, after joining the US trade scheme AGOA in 2001 brought new clothing investment. Growth slowed from 2.6 percent a year in 2006–2015 to 1.6 percent in 2016–2025 while swings in customs revenue strained the budget, and income per person fell in 2018, in the 2020 pandemic, and in 2022, when, the IMF says, government cash shortages slowed building work. It still reached a new high in 2025, after growth of 3.1 percent, with recent growth led by manufacturing, information technology and construction.

threads.title: The sanctions boom and its end
threads.text: In the 1980s, South African and multinational firms set up in Eswatini to get around sanctions on apartheid South Africa. When South Africa opened up in the mid-1990s, many moved back, and investment fell sharply between the 1980s and the 2000s. In 2023 the IMF wrote that the country had still not fully recovered from that loss.

threads.title: Tied to South Africa
threads.text: Eswatini's fortunes move with South Africa's through shared customs revenue and a currency pegged to the rand. The IMF also notes that most of its electricity is imported from South Africa and Mozambique.

since_last_year.text: Growth picked up in 2025 and early 2026, and income per person reached a new high in 2025. At the same time, the budget deficit widened after a public wage review agreed in October 2025, and foreign reserves fell to critically low levels in mid-2026 as imports of fuel and capital goods rose.

growth_story.tension: The sources date Eswatini's slowdown to the end of sanctions in the mid-1990s, but the data find no lasting shift since 1990. Most of the strong sanctions years fall before 1990, when the era test starts, and the slow late 1990s were followed by faster growth in 2002–2007. The World Bank's figure for growth over the past decade measures total output, while income per person grew 1.6 percent a year over 2016–2025; part of that gap is population growth.
